clue.text: Shot from right in cracking cup-tie

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes inside the other before the shuffle
something cracking is breaking apart, so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, minus the hyphen
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A goal scored from the right during a thrilling knockout football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' and 'cracking' both belong to the football picture, but R goes into CUPTIE and the seven letters are rearranged into PICTURE. A cup-tie is a knockout cup match in British football.
explanation.definitionFit: A photograph is commonly called a shot, and a photograph is also a picture, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Settle around Skye? Here's another Scots location

indicators.note: to go around something is to enclose it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: to settle a bill is to pay it
Skye is a Scottish island, an example of an isle

explanation.surface: Someone thinks of settling down on the Isle of Skye, then is offered a different Scottish place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settle' reads as moving house, but it means paying a bill. 'Another' is fair because Skye is itself a Scottish location.
explanation.definitionFit: Paisley is a large town west of Glasgow in Scotland, so it is one more Scottish place name.

clue.text: Very good in bed? Suffer the consequences!

indicators.note: being in something means lying inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
PI is informal short form of pious, very good in the saintly sense

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about performance in bed, followed by a warning that there will be a price to pay.
explanation.walkthrough: PI goes inside COT. 'Very good' is not praise for skill here but piety: PI is crossword shorthand for pious.
explanation.definitionFit: COP IT is British slang meaning to get into trouble or be punished, which is paying the penalty for something.

clue.text: Complete Charlie must leave sailing ship

indicators.note: whatever must leave is taken away, so one letter is removed from the word

parts.note: a cutter is a small fast sailing vessel
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An order that the whole of a sailor named Charlie must get off a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove C from CUTTER. 'Complete' looks like it describes Charlie but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter and complete both mean total or absolute, as in an utter fool or a complete fool.

clue.text: Immortal eastern bird on a lake

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for eastern
a tern is a seabird
taken as written
L is the map abbreviation for lake
placed next in line

explanation.surface: A legendary deathless bird from the East floating on a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: Four simple parts in clue order; 'on' just sets TERN before the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immortal never dies and lasts for ever, which is exactly what eternal means.

clue.text: Greek character nicked old Spanish coin

parts.note: pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
nicked is British slang for stole

explanation.surface: A Greek man pinched an antique Spanish coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' reads like a person, but it is a letter of the alphabet. To nick is British slang for to steal.
explanation.definitionFit: The pistole was a gold coin used in Spain in earlier centuries, a historical piece of money.

clue.text: Stir with black parsley perhaps

parts.note: a pother is a commotion, a stir
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
joins the two parts

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: stir it with some black parsley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir' is a noun here, a fuss, not the kitchen verb. POTHER is an old word for a fuss or disturbance.
explanation.definitionFit: A potherb is any leafy plant grown for flavouring cooking, and parsley is a typical example.

clue.text: Italian serving small soft crackers at eight

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small

indicators.note: crackers means mad or broken up, so the letters go haywire into a new order

parts.note: P is piano, the musical instruction for soft
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Italian waiter brings out small soft biscuits at eight o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crackers' looks like biscuits being served, but it is the signal for rearranging AT EIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is a long thin pasta, a dish typical of Italian cooking, so an Italian serving of food.

clue.text: Runner, old, unexpectedly regains lead in race

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: something happening unexpectedly departs from its expected order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of race

explanation.surface: An elderly runner surprisingly takes the lead again in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' is not an athlete but someone who runs an event.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who runs an event or business manages and arranges it, so a runner in that sense is an organiser.

clue.text: Refusal to receive student is picked up in letter

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top
to receive something is to take it in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: nope is an informal refusal
L is a learner, on a learner driver's plate
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student is refused entry, and the refusal is overheard in a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' suggests hearing something, but in a down clue it means lifted, so the built word reads from the bottom upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth character of the Greek alphabet, so it is a letter.

clue.text: Anxious, I'm one receiving medical care

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
a patient is a person being treated by doctors

explanation.surface: Someone admits to being nervous because they are in hospital being treated.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a patient is the one who should not be impatient.
explanation.definitionFit: Anxious here means eager or restless to get on, which is the sense of being unwilling to wait.

clue.text: Support US soldier in ebbing sea

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other
the tide ebbing flows back out, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: taken as written
GI is the familiar name for an American soldier

explanation.surface: Backing an American serviceman adrift in a retreating tide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' could be a verb, but the answer is a noun meaning protection; the ebbing tide simply turns its word around.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the aegis of someone means under their protection or sponsorship, so the word means backing or patronage.

clue.text: Roman palace in more recent article

parts.note: later means more recent
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A Roman palace is featured in a recent magazine article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the grammatical kind, not a piece of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lateran Palace in Rome was for centuries the chief residence of the popes, a famous papal palace.

clue.text: Restructuring the loan makes you solvent

indicators.note: restructuring a thing rebuilds it in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Financial advice: rescheduling your debt keeps you out of the red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solvent' in finance means able to pay debts; in the answer it is the chemistry sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethanol is alcohol, widely used in industry and laboratories as a liquid that dissolves other substances.

clue.text: The solver is leaving this card in leisure centre

parts.note: the solver is you, the reader

indicators.note: whatever is leaving goes away, so those letters are taken out of the word

parts.note: taken as written, before its I and S are removed
taken as written; these are the letters removed
a club is a playing card of one suit

explanation.surface: The crossword solver drops a playing card off at the sports centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' is not a verb but the pair of letters removed from THIS. Crossword clues often call the solver 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: A youth club is a place where young people meet for games and activities in their free time.

clue.text: A French work put forward not challenged

parts.note: un is French for a
OP is opus, a musical work
to pose a question is to put it forward

explanation.surface: A French piece of writing is submitted and nobody disputes it.
explanation.walkthrough: OP is the standard abbreviation of opus in catalogues of music.
explanation.definitionFit: When nobody stands against a candidate or proposal it goes through without objection, which is being unopposed.

clue.text: Powerful explosive with nuclear particles?

parts.note: HE is high explosive

indicators.note: broken into particles means smashed to bits, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
joins the two parts

explanation.surface: A mighty bomb built with atomic particles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuclear particles' reads as physics, but the question mark hints that the word NUCLEAR is itself broken into pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercules was the strongest hero of Greek myth, so something Herculean has enormous strength or needs great effort.

clue.text: Boxer starts to train young lad

indicators.note: the start of each word is its opening letter, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words
a son is a lad, a boy

explanation.surface: A boxer begins coaching a young boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' reads as 'begins to', but it picks out the first letters of the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Mike Tyson was a world heavyweight boxing champion, one of the best-known fighters of all time.

clue.text: Almost axe Irish singing group

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to axe is to chop; the last letter goes
IR is the abbreviation for Irish

explanation.surface: An Irish vocal ensemble is nearly shut down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axe' is the verb, to chop, cut short by one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A choir is an organised body of people who sing together, often in a church or school.

clue.text: More tea houses where Sloane Square is located

indicators.note: a building houses its occupants by holding them within, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: cha is British slang for tea
else means more, as in anything else

explanation.surface: A smart London district with more tea rooms around its famous square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' is a verb, not the buildings. CHA for tea is old British slang, borrowed from Chinese.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloane Square is a square in the Chelsea district of west London, so the answer names its location.

clue.text: Festival to enjoy with artist in sweet bar?

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so the joined pair goes within the other piece

parts.note: a Mars bar is a chocolate bar
to dig something is slang for liking it
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
joins the two inner parts

explanation.surface: A celebration where you enjoy yourself alongside a painter at a candy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A Mars bar is a well-known British chocolate bar, and RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Mardi Gras is the carnival held on Shrove Tuesday, most famously in New Orleans, so it is a festival.

clue.text: An expert in safe delivery?

parts.note: surface reading: a courier skilled at getting parcels through intact
setter's reading: someone trained to bring babies into the world safely

explanation.walkthrough: Delivery suggests post or couriers; the question mark flags the other sense, delivering a baby.
explanation.definitionFit: This professional is a trained health worker who assists women during childbirth, making the birth safe.

clue.text: Calm end to summer with flutes playing

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the last letter of summer

indicators.note: playing means performing or moving about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
joins the two parts

explanation.surface: A peaceful late-summer evening accompanied by flutes.
explanation.walkthrough: The final letter of summer comes first, then FLUTES rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Restful and calm both describe something quiet, peaceful and soothing.

clue.text: Lieutenant in complete retreat

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: sheer means complete, as in sheer madness
LT is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: A lieutenant leads his troops in a full withdrawal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' reads as a military verb but is a noun, a place of refuge.
explanation.definitionFit: A retreat is a quiet safe place to withdraw to, which is a shelter or refuge.

clue.text: Lover no longer needing money set out

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
the pound is British money
joins the two parts

explanation.surface: A former lover who no longer needs cash has left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' seems to mean departed, but it means to explain in detail.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound an idea is to present and explain it fully, as one sets out an argument.

clue.text: Scene rewritten keeps one line still

indicators.note: to keep is to hold on to, so one piece holds the other inside
writing something again produces a new version, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A redrafted theatre scene still retains one of its lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adverb but is a verb, to quieten.
explanation.definitionFit: To still a crowd or a noise is to quieten it, which is the verb to silence.

clue.text: Six-footer to be left with Bible in AA

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: taken as written
RV is the Revised Version of the Bible
joins the parts

explanation.surface: A tall person heading into Alcoholics Anonymous takes a Bible along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it is a creature with six legs, like a caterpillar. RV goes between the two As.
explanation.definitionFit: Insects have six legs, and an insect grub or caterpillar is a larva, so a six-legged creature.

clue.text: Excellent opener from Huddersfield Town

parts.note: neat is slang for excellent

indicators.note: an opener is what comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of Huddersfield

explanation.surface: A fine first goal from Huddersfield Town, the English football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Huddersfield Town' is a football club name, but 'Town' is split off as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Neath is an industrial town in south Wales, near Swansea, so it is simply an example of a town.

clue.text: Woman's soiree regularly involving us

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one piece encloses the other
at regular intervals means every other letter, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman's evening party often includes the two of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman's' is read as 'woman is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Susie is a common female first name, so it is an example of a woman.

clue.text: Rat popular with staff in castle

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a fort is a fortified building, like a castle
to staff a post is to man it
joins the parts

explanation.surface: A rat is a favourite of the servants in the castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rat' is not the rodent but a traitor, and 'staff' is a verb meaning to provide people for a post.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat on someone is to tell tales to the authorities, so a rat is an informer or informant.

clue.text: An Italian poet is rather slow

parts.note: taken as written
Dante wrote the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: A dig at an Italian poet for being a bit sluggish.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian theme fits: the answer is an Italian musical term.
explanation.definitionFit: Andante is a musical tempo marking meaning at a moderately slow, walking pace.

clue.text: Hide the mad king outside!

indicators.note: being outside something means wrapping around it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: King Lear goes mad in Shakespeare's play
taken as written

explanation.surface: A command to conceal something by leaving the deranged king out in the open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like a verb but is a noun, animal skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Hide is an animal's skin, and tanned hide is leather, so the two nouns match.
